umf.visual.title: UMF access across engine boundaries
umf.visual.question: Which parts of the documented access stack own protocols, execution and pinned reads?
umf.visual.takeaway: A documented target design: UMF owns protocols and clients; each engine owns its protected adapter paths. Native capability qualification remains separate.
omissions: This is the documented adapter boundary design, not a deployment or a claim that every target capability is implemented or qualified.
Raw-table targets and Weft catalog compilation are outside this focused engine-adapter view.

annotations.text: The conformance boundary that lets Truss and Ashlar act as SDK targets. UMF owns the protocols, the conformance suite, the adoption packet shape and the engine-specific witness list. Each engine owns its adapter, its adoption design and its execution authority. This design changes no engine storage and amends no sibling contract.

Selected: engines implement the same target protocols as raw tables, over their own protected paths. Weft compiles catalog entries for each engine through its existing backend. The adapter adds no semantics: it routes catalog entries and encoded inputs into the engine and maps results back to SDK outcomes.
Rejected: Latest-table reads on Ashlar. They can mix table versions from different publications. Every read is resolver-pinned instead.
Rejected: Ashlar actions or bulk through the SDK. Ashlar writes, ACK progress and publication are its own protocol. Ashlar provides no `ActionExecutor` or `BulkTarget`.
